item.title: Guide to Building a Local AI Stack. Part 6. Converting Hugging Face Models to GGUF
item.description:
Not all models exist in the ready-made .gguf format. Sometimes you need a model that the community hasn't quantized yet, or you want a specific quantization (Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0) that isn't available in pre-built versions. In such cases, you need to convert it yourself: from raw Hugging Face weights (.safetensors) to GGUF, and then to the desired quantization. The convert_to_gguf.sh script automates the entire process: from installing dependencies to the final .gguf file, with cleanup of intermediate data. Read more

item.title: From Clicker to Multi-Agent System: How Test Automation Evolved and What's Next
item.description:
Hi Habr! My name is Ilya Baranov, and I'm a testing lead at Sber Disk. I've been involved in test automation for many years, progressing from simple clickers to modern multi-agent systems. Let's trace this evolution. I'll present the material not chronologically, but in the order I encountered and mastered various technologies and products. I want to share my experience, not just list automation tools, focusing on the problems and tasks I solved with these technologies. Read on.

item.title: I asked 14 neural networks to help my mom reply to an OLX seller. All 14 helped her send prepayment to a scammer
item.description:
Ask a neural network "is this a scam?" — and almost any will answer correctly: the 14 models I tested scored between 0.93 and 1.00. Now ask the same models: "write a polite reply to the seller that I agree to prepay and will transfer today" — about the classic OLX scheme. Out of 42 replies, all 42 wrote the message. Only five added a warning — and that was after the ready-made text that a person would copy and send. I'll tell you how I assembled a benchmark of 72 scam and real messages in Russian, Kazakh, and Shala, what Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and others showed — and why "recognize a scammer" and "warn about them" turned out to be two different skills. Read more

item.title: Code as Policy: How LLMs Control Robots Through Generated Code
item.description:
Hello, Habr! Today we'll discuss how neural networks can effectively control robots using an approach that might not seem obvious at first glance. In 2023, Alphabet shut down the Everyday Robots project, which attempted to create a robot for cleaning offices and sorting trash. Unfortunately, the androids proved incapable of performing tasks in the complex and ever-changing environment of human spaces. However, this effort led to the development of Code as Policy (CaP) technology, which has continued to evolve as a separate direction. Its principle is simple: an LLM writes the code that controls the manipulator. Let's explore how the CaP approach works and how it's evaluated by the new CodeActionBench benchmark, released in late September. We'll also look at where the method works, where it fails, and why the "robot that programs itself" is no longer just a marketing slogan. Read on

item.title: File converter that opens on drag-and-drop: how I made Kumquat for macOS without Xcode
item.description:
I drag a file into Finder, briefly press Shift, and a wheel of actions opens under the cursor: 'to JPG', 'compress to 2MB', 'recognize text', 'merge to PDF'. I drop the file onto a petal, and the result appears next to the original. I'll explain how to catch such a gesture without Accessibility permissions, why I had to compile ffmpeg and nine codecs from source, how much faster VideoToolbox is than libx264, and how it was all written with Anthropic's Claude. Read more

item.title: [Translation] How Codemode is Changing AI Agents' Interaction with Tools — and What's Wrong with MCP
item.description:
When an AI agent needs to work with dozens of tools, each call and its result can create an excessive load on the LLM's context. Codemode allows combining operations in code, but working with MCP introduces new limitations — from nested calls to unpredictable response formats. Using Pi as an example, we'll explore how Codemode changes the architecture of agent systems, what MCP problems it helps solve, and where the approach itself falters. Understanding Codemode.

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: How We Taught a Neural Network to Detect Deepfakes and Explain Its Verdict
item.description:
Generative AI is changing lives, but not always for the better. Scammers use audio deepfakes to defraud people. Reliable Speech Deepfake Detection (SDD) is crucial, but current methods lack universality and interpretability. We developed HIR-SDD, combining large audio-language models with human-annotated reasoning. This method explains why audio is deemed real or fake, providing human-understandable cues. Our approach, presented at Interspeech, integrates large audio-language models with step-by-step reasoning derived from human-labeled data. This article details our method, experimental results, and why "I don't hear synthesis artifacts" doesn't guarantee a real voice.

item.title: How much does an AI bot for business cost in 2026: calculating with GigaChat and YandexGPT prices
item.description:
When an entrepreneur asks how much an AI bot for a website or messenger costs, they usually get two answers. The developer names the development price, and about the monthly costs for the neural network itself, they say "pennies." Both answers are incomplete. Development is paid once, and the model charges for each response to the client, and after six months, this budget line can become noticeable. Read more

item.title: Fifteen Claude Code sessions ate 11 GB of RAM. I wrote a mod that shows who exactly
item.description:
I usually have ten to fifteen Claude Code sessions open. Each has its own sub-agents and MCP servers, some with Vite running, others with pytest. For a while, this worked fine, but then my 64GB machine started struggling with every window switch. I opened the task manager and saw a wall of identical node and claude processes. You can see how much they consume, but not who they belong to. That's how claude-load was born, a mod for Claude Code that breaks down machine load by session. The very first run showed 15 active sessions consuming a total of 10.8 GB. I'll explain how the mod identifies process ownership, why the 'terminate' button turned out to be the most dangerous part of the project, and what pitfalls I encountered in the new Claude Code mods. Read on

item.title: Pydantic AI: Typed Agents on Your Models
item.description:
The typical project with an LLM agent follows a similar fate. Initially, it's a neat forty lines: a prompt, a call to an OpenAI-compatible API, json.loads — and it works. A couple of weeks later, the model starts inserting explanatory text before the JSON, like "Sure! Here's your answer:", one of the mandatory fields sometimes appears and sometimes disappears, and a nested array occasionally comes as a string. Regular expressions, manual checks, and retries creep into the code. Another month later, you own a few hundred lines of glue code that no one wants to touch because it's unclear what exactly will break. Alas, the model is often not to blame here. The connection between its output and the application breaks — where there are neither types nor format validation. Pydantic AI offers a way out of this cycle through type models. The framework is made by the Pydantic team — the very library that powers validation in FastAPI, OpenAI SDK, and a dozen other projects. The agent tool is described as a regular function with annotations, the structured response as a pydantic model, and switching from a cloud model to a local one via Ollama is reduced to changing one line. This is what the README says. Below the fold — how it looks in practice. Read on.

item.title: How People Invented Beauty: An Atlas of 195 Visual Styles, from Lascaux Caves to Weirdcore
item.description:
AI has given everyone a superpower: the ability to generate a beautiful image in a minute. But this superpower has fallen into the hands of people who often don't know what to do with it. This includes me. Anyone can ask an AI to 'draw in the style of Impressionism.' But only someone who knows that Neoplasticism or Vaporwave styles exist, and how they differ, can ask for 'in the style of Neoplasticism' or 'in the style of Vaporwave.' It's like being given the ability to build any house with a snap of my fingers. Any. But which one? I haven't studied architecture and will likely build what my neighbor has, not what truly resonates with me. I have no art education. So, I decided to create a map for myself: what visual styles have people invented, where did they come from, and how are they related? This resulted in the Aesthetics Atlas. Explore the atlas.

item.title: Nano Banana 2.1 or ChatGPT Image 2.5: Comparing Image Generation Neural Networks on 5 Identical Prompts
item.description:
Nano Banana 2.1 and ChatGPT Image 2.5 tackle similar tasks: creating images from text prompts and editing existing ones. However, after several generations, it becomes clear that the models err differently. One adheres more precisely to technical specifications, while the other better preserves facial features or creates a more cohesive visual. Comparing such neural networks based on a single beautiful example is pointless. For product imagery, object placement accuracy is more important; for posters, text; for advertising shots, resemblance to a reference; and for editing, the ability to change exactly one element without redrawing everything else.
